original_question: Prove that a simple group of finite Morley rank without involutions cannot act definably, faithfully, and irreducibly on a connected group other than on itself acting by conjugation.
target_in_paper: Problem 21.20 of Section 21 (with the definition of irreducibility taken from the immediately preceding Problem 21.19) in the current arXiv version of Unsolved Problems in Group Theory. The Kourovka Notebook.
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the core mathematical content of the paper-faithful target almost verbatim: the acting group is simple of finite Morley rank, it has no involutions, the action is definable, faithful, and irreducible, the object acted on is a connected group, and the only expected exception is the group's action on itself by conjugation.
missing_details: The paper you pointed to is not a research article with Conjecture 1.1 / Proposition 1.2 / Theorem 1.3 matching this draft; in the current arXiv version of arXiv:1401.0300, the draft corresponds directly to Problem 21.20.
The target of the action should also be stated to be a group of finite Morley rank, not just a connected group.
The action should be made explicit as an action by definable automorphisms of the target group.
The meaning of irreducible is not self-contained in Problem 21.20; Problem 21.19 supplies it: there is no definable non-trivial proper invariant subgroup of the acted-upon group.
The phrase without involutions should be stated explicitly as containing no element of order 2.
The phrase acting by conjugation should be formalized as the standard inner action of the simple group on itself.

The phrase equivalent to the action on itself by conjugation should be spelled out as existence of a definable isomorphism between the target group and the acting group that intertwines the given action with conjugation.
refined_question: Let G and V be groups of finite Morley rank. Assume that G is a simple group with no involutions, that V is connected, and that G acts definably and faithfully on V by automorphisms. Assume further that the action is irreducible, in the sense that V has no definable non-trivial proper G-invariant subgroup. Prove that the only possible such action is the standard conjugation action of G on itself: namely, V is definably isomorphic to G, and under some definable isomorphism V ≅ G the given action of G on V corresponds to the action of G on itself by conjugation.
justification: In the current arXiv version of 1401.0300, your draft matches Problem 21.20 essentially word for word. The only paper-critical hidden assumption is the definition of irreducible, which is given immediately above in Problem 21.19. Since Problem 21.20 itself leaves several notions implicit, the refined version makes explicit that both groups are of finite Morley rank, that the action is by definable automorphisms, that irreducibility means no definable non-trivial proper invariant subgroup, and that equivalence with conjugation means an intertwining definable isomorphism V ≅ G. This keeps the scope exactly at the level of the notebook problem and does not broaden it.
